data.title: Secret Shapes All Around Us
data.description: A 3-part narrated walkthrough with a check after each part.

segments.title: Spotting a Round Clock
segments.script: Benny Bear looks up at the kitchen wall and spots a ticking clock. Its border curves all the way around with no corners at all. That round clock is shaped just like a circle!
segments.imagePrompt: A friendly cartoon bear named Benny standing in a bright kitchen, happily pointing up to a round wall clock. The circular rim of the clock glows with a soft yellow outline. Storybook illustration style with clean lines and warm pastel colors.

knowledgeCheck.question: What shape is hiding in Benny's wall clock?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The clock curves all the way around with no corners, so it is a circle.

segments.title: Finding a Square Window
segments.script: Next, Benny looks at the sunny playroom window. It has four straight sides that are all the exact same size, with four matching corners. The window is shaped just like a square!
segments.imagePrompt: Benny Bear looking happily at a bright square window in a cozy playroom. Outside the window, a green garden is visible. The four equal sides of the square window frame are highlighted with a soft, cheerful glow. Friendly children's book art style.

knowledgeCheck.question: What shape did Benny find in the window?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The window has four straight sides of the exact same size, so it is a square.

segments.title: Snacking on Triangle Pizza
segments.script: Time for lunch, so Benny picks up a warm slice of pizza. He counts three straight sides and three pointy corners at the crust and tip. That yummy pizza slice is shaped like a triangle!
segments.imagePrompt: Benny Bear sitting at a small wooden table holding up a single triangular slice of cheese pizza. The three straight sides and three pointed corners of the slice are highlighted with gentle sparkle lines. Fun, vibrant storybook illustration for young children.

knowledgeCheck.question: What shape is Benny's yummy slice of pizza?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The pizza slice has three straight sides and three pointy corners, making it a triangle.

data.title: Home Shape Detectives: The Great 2D Shape Hunt
data.subject: Math
data.topic: Identifying and Describing 2D Shapes (Circles, Squares, Rectangles, Triangles)
data.overview: Grab your detective magnifying glass and explore your home! In this hands-on mission, young learners will touch, trace, and hunt down real-world circles, squares, rectangles, and triangles hidden in plain sight.
learningObjectives: Identify and name four basic 2D geometric shapes: circle, square, rectangle, and triangle.
Count the sides and corners (vertices) of everyday objects to sort them into shape categories.
Distinguish between squares and rectangles by comparing side lengths.

steps.title: Make Your Shape Badges
steps.instruction: Draw one big shape on each of your four pieces of paper: a circle on the first, a square on the second, a rectangle on the third, and a triangle on the fourth. Write the shape name with a helper.
steps.tip: Trace a cup or a coaster if you want help drawing a very neat circle!

steps.title: Inspect the Clues: Sides and Corners
steps.instruction: Run your finger along each drawn shape. Count its straight sides, and touch its pointy corners. Notice that the circle is round and smooth with no straight sides or corners at all.

checkpoint.question: How many pointy corners does your triangle have?

steps.scienceNote: Shapes are defined by their rules! A corner (or vertex) is where two straight lines meet.

steps.title: Hunt for Round Circles
steps.instruction: Grab your bag and walk through the room looking for objects with round circle faces. Gently pick them up or point them out, tracing the round rim with your pointer finger.
steps.tip: Look at the lids of jars, round drink coasters, or clock faces.

steps.title: Hunt for Straight-Sided Squares and Rectangles
steps.instruction: Search for objects with four straight sides. Find one item where all four sides are equal length (a square) and one item where two sides are long and two are short (a rectangle).

checkpoint.question: Can you confirm that both your square object and rectangle object have 4 corners?

steps.scienceNote: Squares are a special type of rectangle where every single side is the exact same length.

steps.title: The Tricky Triangle Search
steps.instruction: Triangles can be sneaky detectives! Look for things that have 3 straight sides and 3 pointy corners, like a wedge of cheese, a folded napkin, a roof shape outside a window, or a musical triangle.
steps.tip: If you cannot find a triangle object, fold a square paper napkin diagonally across the center to create one!

steps.title: Shape Sorting Station
steps.instruction: Lay out your four shape badges on the floor or a table. Place each discovered item next to its matching shape badge, forming four shape collections.

checkpoint.question: Which shape badge has the biggest pile of collected items?

reflectionPrompts.question: What felt different when you traced the edge of a circle compared to tracing the edge of a square?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Distinguish between curved and straight-sided 2D shapes
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about whether your finger went smoothly in a curve or had to stop and turn at a corner.

reflectionPrompts.question: How can you tell if an object with four sides is a square or a rectangle?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Distinguish between squares and rectangles by comparing side lengths
reflectionPrompts.hint: Look closely at the sides: are they all twins of the same length, or are two longer?

reflectionPrompts.question: Why do you think doors and books are shaped like rectangles instead of circles?
reflectionPrompts.connectionTo: Identify and name four basic 2D geometric shapes in the real world
reflectionPrompts.hint: Think about how books stack together or how a round door might swing open.

documentationPrompt.instruction: Take a photo of all your hunted objects arranged neatly around their matching shape badges on the floor.
documentationPrompt.suggestedCaption: I became a Shape Detective! I found [number] objects. My favorite shape to hunt was the [circle/square/rectangle/triangle] because [reason].

extensions.title: Body Shape Builders
extensions.description: Use your arms, fingers, or your whole body on the rug to bend and stretch into a triangle, a rectangle, or a circle with a family member!

extensions.title: Tape Town Walk
extensions.description: Have an adult tape large outlines of the shapes on the floor using painter's tape. Walk like an animal along each shape's perimeter (e.g., hop around the circle, stomp along the 4 square sides).

safetyNotes: Adult helper recommended: Supervise children while collecting household items.
Do not collect fragile, sharp, or breakable items (such as glass plates, knives, or ceramic mugs).
Keep exploration away from stairwells, electrical outlets, and high shelves.

challenges.instruction: Can you build a shape with 3 straight sides and 3 corners? Let's make a triangle!
challenges.hint: Try connecting three dots to make three straight sides that meet at three corners.
challenges.narration: Welcome! Let's start by building a shape with 3 sides and 3 corners. Can you connect the dots?

challenges.instruction: Great job! Now let's build a shape with 4 straight sides and 4 corners.
challenges.hint: Count four sides as you connect the dots. All four corners should look nice and square!
challenges.narration: Awesome! Next, let's try making a shape with 4 sides and 4 corners.

problems.question: Which shape is a triangle?
problems.rationale: A triangle is a shape with three straight sides and three corners. The shape with three pointed corners is the triangle. Circles are curved and round, while squares have four straight sides.
problems.teachingNote: Have students practice counting the three corners and three sides of triangles using their fingers to reinforce the concept.
successCriteria: Identify a triangle from basic two-dimensional shapes.
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.rationale: A circle is round and has a smooth, curved line all the way around it. It does not have any straight sides or sharp corners like a square or triangle.
problems.teachingNote: Kindergarten students often confuse round shapes with flat-sided shapes when learning basic geometry. Help them feel the smooth curve of a circle with their finger to reinforce that it has no straight edges.
successCriteria: Identify the defining attribute of a circle as a curved shape
Distinguish between curved boundaries and straight sides
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Which shape has four corners?
problems.rationale: A square has four straight sides and four pointy corners. A circle has round sides with no corners, and a triangle only has three corners. That makes the square the shape with four corners!
problems.teachingNote: Encourage young learners to count corners by touching each pointy tip on real-world blocks or shape cutouts.
successCriteria: Identify shapes that have four corners
Distinguish a square from shapes with zero or three corners
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Which of these looks like a circle?
problems.rationale: A wall clock is round and curved with no corners, which makes it a circle. Books and doors have straight sides and corners, so they look like rectangles instead.
problems.teachingNote: Have students trace the edge of a classroom clock in the air with their finger to reinforce that circles are round curves with zero corners.
successCriteria: Identify a familiar real-world object shaped like a circle

detectedConstraints.description: In obj2-tracer-finger-draw, all four challenges have targetShape set to triangle despite instructions directing the student to trace circles, squares, and rectangles.
Objective obj3 lacks sufficient direct assessment items comparing shapes by sides and corners, with only one comparative multiple-choice question provided.

coverage.summary: The lesson effectively teaches and assesses shape recognition in everyday objects (obj1) and basic shape naming (obj2) through interactive listening checks and spoken identification tasks covering circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles. However, comparing shapes by attributes (obj3) is insufficiently assessed; the interactive sorter and builder blocks focus on isolated counting and polygon construction rather than active comparison, leaving only a single multiple-choice question to assess the comparative skill.
